summary:
Scout Ahead is a Marswalk planner for the boxwork ridges of Mount Sharp in Gale Crater. Before the astronaut sets out, a robotic scout checks the ground along the route and pins what it finds on the map: clear, go with care, or no go.

At each of 60 stops the scout classifies the terrain in its camera photos with a model trained on NASA's AI4Mars data, picks the safest of seven candidate paths, and has a second method with no AI check its work. If the two disagree, the stop is never marked clear. The map adds steep ground and drop-offs from NASA's 1 m elevation model, the weather Curiosity measured there, radiation dose, and the time to walk back.

The scout is a replay of a real Curiosity drive (sols 4600-4893), so every photo, position and weather reading is real NASA data. The model scores 92.3% pixel accuracy on NASA's expert-labeled test set.

An astronaut on foot cannot see past the next ridge, and orbital images cannot tell firm bedrock from loose sand. A scout that goes first can.
details:
THE PROBLEM

An astronaut on foot cannot see what is past the next ridge, and orbital images cannot tell firm bedrock from loose sand. Sand traps and rock fields cost time, and time on a Marswalk is oxygen. A robot that goes first can look at the ground up close.

WHAT SCOUT AHEAD DOES

1. Plans from orbit. It reads NASA's 1 m HiRISE elevation model for the walk area, marks slopes over 15 and 25 degrees and drops of more than 1.5 m, and rates each leg of the route as gentle, steep in places, or go around.

2. Sends a scout. The scout stops 60 times along a 1.14 km route. At each stop it looks at up to four photos: ahead, right, behind and left. In this demo the scout is a replay of Curiosity's drive through the boxwork ridges on sols 4600-4893.

3. Checks the ground twice. A U-Net segmentation model, trained on NASA JPL's AI4Mars labels, colours each photo as soil, bedrock, sand or big rock. A separate classical computer-vision check, with no machine learning, finds rocks by their shadows and smooth ground by its lack of texture. When the two disagree, the stop is never marked clear.

4. Picks a path. Seven candidate paths fan out across each photo. Each is scored by the share of sand and rock it crosses. At Stop A the straight path is 23% sand and rock, so the scout picks a path to the left at 6%.

5. Briefs the astronaut. Every stop shows a verdict (go, go with care, no go), the time to walk back to the start, air and ground temperature and pressure from Curiosity's weather station on that sol, slope, and radiation dose so far.

HOW WELL IT WORKS

On NASA's expert-labeled AI4Mars test set (322 images the model never saw), the model scores 92.3% pixel accuracy and 0.67 mean IoU. It is good at soil (0.91), sand (0.86) and bedrock (0.81) and poor at big rocks (0.11), which is why the second check exists. Elevation from orbit matches Curiosity's own position data to within 0.4 m at all 60 stops.

WHY IT IS CREATIVE

It does not trust its own AI. Two independent methods must agree before a stop is called clear. And instead of simulating a robot, it replays a real one: every photo, position and weather reading comes from Curiosity.

WHAT IS HONEST ABOUT IT

The site says what is real and what is not. The scout is a replay, not a live robot. Terrain colours are predictions. Walking speed and slope limits are our assumptions. Radiation is a long-term average with no solar storm alerts. Path picking is 2D, in the photo, with no depth.

HOW IT WAS BUILT

Python does all the model work ahead of time and saves images and JSON. The site is a static Leaflet page on GitHub Pages with NASA Mars Trek tiles as the basemap. Tools: Python, PyTorch, segmentation-models-pytorch, OpenCV, rasterio, Leaflet. Trained on one RTX 2070 SUPER.

WHAT COMES NEXT

Stereo depth from the navigation camera pairs, so the chosen path can be placed on the map. A scored test of the edge check. A live rover in place of the replay.

Live site: https://lorenzodemarni.github.io/mars-scout/

Code: https://github.com/LorenzoDeMarni/mars-scout
